questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old male with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with vomiting and breathlessness. ABG shows: pH 7.22, PaCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 9 mEq/L, PaO2 98 mmHg. Serum electrolytes: Na 138, K 5.2, Cl 100 mEq/L. Blood glucose is 480 mg/dL with large ketonuria. What is the anion gap and what does it indicate?

options.A: Anion gap 16 mEq/L — normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
options.B: Anion gap 29 mEq/L — high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to ketoacidosis
options.C: Anion gap 12 mEq/L — mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Anion gap 22 mEq/L — lactic acidosis from sepsis

questions.explanation: Anion Gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 138 - (100 + 9) = 29 mEq/L (normal 8-12 mEq/L). High AG >12 indicates accumulation of unmeasured anions. MUDPILES mnemonic covers causes: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, INH/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates. Here, DKA causes ketoacid accumulation → high AG metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul breathing (deep rapid respirations) is the compensatory respiratory response. Expected compensation: PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2 = 21.5 (actual 24 — adequate compensation).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old female on hydrochlorothiazide presents with nausea, confusion, and serum sodium of 118 mEq/L. She appears euvolemic. Serum osmolality is 245 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 42 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis and why is rapid correction dangerous?

options.A: Psychogenic polydipsia — risk of hypernatremia with correction
options.B: SIADH — risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) with rapid correction
options.C: Hypothyroidism — risk of myxedema coma with diuresis
options.D: Cerebral salt wasting — risk of hypovolemic shock with fluid restriction

questions.explanation: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH secretion) presents with: hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, euvolemia, high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg, here 480), high urine sodium (>40 mEq/L) in a clinically euvolemic patient. Thiazides impair diluting ability, commonly precipitating SIADH. The critical danger of rapid correction (>8-10 mEq/L/24 hours) is Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS/Central Pontine Myelinolysis) — neurons in a chronically adapted low-osmolality environment shrink rapidly when osmolality rises fast, causing demyelination, locked-in syndrome, and death. Correct at ≤8 mEq/L/day using fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male presents 18 hours after consuming illicitly produced alcohol with severe visual disturbance ('looking through a snowstorm'), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.18, HCO3 8), and high anion gap (AG 28). Osmol gap is elevated. Fundoscopy shows optic disc hyperemia. Which enzyme is responsible for the toxic metabolite formation, and what is the specific antidote?

options.A: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol to formaldehyde/formic acid — antidote: fomepizole or ethanol
options.B: CYP2E1 converts methanol directly to formate — antidote: N-acetylcysteine
options.C: Aldehyde dehydrogenase converts methanol to methanol acetaldehyde — antidote: disulfiram
options.D: Catalase converts methanol to carbon monoxide — antidote: hydroxocobalamin

questions.explanation: Methanol (wood alcohol) itself is non-toxic — it is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to formaldehyde, then aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid (formate). Formate is the toxic metabolite causing: optic nerve toxicity (blindness — pathognomonic), high AG metabolic acidosis, and elevated osmol gap (unmeasured methanol elevates measured osmolality). Antidotes: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) — ADH inhibitor, preferred; or IV Ethanol (competes for ADH). Hemodialysis removes methanol and formate directly. Folinic acid enhances formate metabolism. Act fast — visual damage is irreversible.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male with COPD and cor pulmonale is admitted with worsening dyspnea. ABG: pH 7.38, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 34 mEq/L, PaO2 56 mmHg. What is the correct interpretation of this ABG?

options.A: Acute respiratory acidosis with no compensation
options.B: Chronic respiratory acidosis with adequate renal compensation — fully compensated
options.C: Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis

questions.explanation: pH is normal (7.38) — but always check if this is truly normal or compensated. Primary disorder: high PaCO2 (58) = respiratory acidosis. Expected renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis: HCO3 increases by 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 above 40. Rise in PaCO2 = 18 mmHg → expected HCO3 rise = 18/10 × 3.5 = 6.3 → expected HCO3 = 40 + 6.3 = ~34 mEq/L. Actual HCO3 = 34 — exactly as expected. Conclusion: chronic (compensated) respiratory acidosis with full renal compensation. Normal pH in a COPD patient does NOT mean normal — always calculate expected compensation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old diabetic male on ACE inhibitor therapy presents with weakness. Serum K is 7.2 mEq/L. ECG shows peaked T waves, widened QRS (180 ms), and a sine wave pattern. What is the correct sequence of emergency management?

options.B: IV calcium gluconate → insulin + dextrose → sodium bicarbonate → salbutamol → kayexalate/hemodialysis
options.C: Insulin + dextrose → calcium gluconate → furosemide → dietary restriction
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate → calcium gluconate → hemodialysis → insulin

questions.explanation: Life-threatening hyperkalemia (K >6.5 + ECG changes): management follows a 3-step sequence — (1) MEMBRANE STABILIZATION: IV calcium gluconate (10 mL 10%) acts within 1-3 minutes — stabilizes cardiac membrane against arrhythmia (does NOT lower K); (2) SHIFT K INTO CELLS: Insulin + dextrose (most reliable, onset 15-30 min) + sodium bicarbonate (if acidosis) + salbutamol nebulization; (3) REMOVE K FROM BODY: Furosemide (if urine output), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (kayexalate), or hemodialysis (fastest and most definitive for severe/refractory cases). Calcium gluconate is always FIRST when ECG changes are present.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old male with recurrent peptic ulcer disease is tested for H. pylori eradication 6 weeks after completing triple therapy. Which diagnostic test for H. pylori offers the highest sensitivity and specificity for confirming eradication in this non-invasive setting, and what is its principle?

options.A: Serology (IgG antibody) — detects antibodies that fall after eradication
options.B: 13C-Urea breath test — H. pylori urease cleaves labeled urea releasing 13CO2 detected in exhaled breath
options.C: Stool antigen test — detects H. pylori antigens using monoclonal antibody ELISA
options.D: Rapid urease test (CLO test) — requires endoscopic biopsy, highly specific

questions.explanation: The 13C-Urea Breath Test (UBT) is the gold standard non-invasive test to confirm H. pylori eradication. Principle: patient ingests 13C-labeled urea — if H. pylori is present, its urease enzyme cleaves the urea to 13CO2 + NH3; 13CO2 is absorbed into blood and exhaled, detected by mass spectrometry/isotope ratio analysis. Sensitivity and specificity >95%. Serology is unreliable for eradication confirmation (antibodies remain elevated for months-years post-eradication). Stool antigen test (monoclonal) is an acceptable alternative for eradication testing. Both UBT and stool antigen require stopping PPIs 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before testing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male with 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with a painless, swollen, warm right foot. Despite the severe deformity on X-ray (fragmentation, subluxation, and sclerosis of the tarsometatarsal joints — 'bag of bones' appearance), the patient reports minimal pain. Peripheral sensations are markedly reduced bilaterally. What is the pathophysiological mechanism of bone destruction in this condition?

options.A: Direct bacterial invasion of bone causing osteomyelitis
options.B: Repetitive microtrauma to insensate joints causing progressive bony destruction via neurovascular reflex
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of synovium by anti-CCP antibodies
options.D: Avascular necrosis from arterial occlusion in diabetic vasculopathy

questions.explanation: Charcot Neuropathic Arthropathy (Charcot foot) results from repetitive microtrauma to joints with severely impaired proprioception and pain sensation (peripheral neuropathy in diabetes). Two theories: (1) Neurotraumatic: loss of protective pain sensation → continued weight bearing on injured joints → progressive destruction; (2) Neurovascular: autonomic neuropathy → increased blood flow → osteoclast activation → bone resorption. The hallmark is a painless (or minimally painful) warm swollen foot with severe radiological destruction — the discordance between clinical appearance and patient symptoms is the key diagnostic clue. Most common site: tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 72-year-old male with Parkinson's disease and diabetes presents with recurrent dizziness and near-syncope on standing. BP supine: 148/88 mmHg; BP after 3 minutes standing: 106/62 mmHg. Heart rate does not change significantly on standing. What does the absence of a compensatory heart rate rise indicate about the mechanism?

options.A: Adequate baroreceptor reflex with peripheral vasoconstriction compensating
options.B: Autonomic neuropathy causing failure of both sympathetic vasoconstriction and cardiac acceleration
options.C: Beta-blocker effect reducing heart rate response to hypotension
options.D: Excessive venous pooling overcome by compensatory tachycardia

questions.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is defined as a drop in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. In neurogenic OH (autonomic failure — as in Parkinson's disease and diabetic autonomic neuropathy), both limbs of the baroreflex fail: (1) Sympathetic efferents fail → no compensatory vasoconstriction → BP drops; (2) Cardiac sympathetics fail → no compensatory tachycardia → heart rate remains fixed. The absence of reflex tachycardia is the key clinical clue distinguishing neurogenic OH from volume depletion (where tachycardia is expected). Treatment: fludrocortisone, midodrine, increased salt/fluid intake.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 19-year-old male presents with tremor, dysarthria, and behavioral changes. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown rings at the outer corneal periphery in Descemet membrane. Serum ceruloplasmin is 6 mg/dL. Which of the following systemic conditions is also associated with Kayser-Fleischer-like corneal copper deposition (pseudo-KF rings) and must be excluded?

options.B: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) with chronic cholestasis

questions.explanation: True Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings are golden-brown copper deposits in Descemet membrane of the peripheral cornea, best seen on slit-lamp, and are pathognomonic for Wilson disease in the context of neurological involvement. However, pseudo-KF rings can appear in conditions causing chronic cholestasis with copper retention (impaired biliary copper excretion) — most importantly Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and other chronic cholestatic liver diseases. Therefore, KF rings alone are not diagnostic of Wilson disease without biochemical confirmation (low ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hr urine copper). In this neurologically affected young patient with low ceruloplasmin, Wilson disease is confirmed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old mountaineer is rescued after 18 hours of exposure in a snowstorm. His fingers are hard, white, and anesthetic. After rescue and rewarming, clear blisters form over the dorsal fingers. Core temperature is now 36.8°C. Hospital imaging with technetium-99m bone scan shows absent perfusion in two digits. Which of the following is the most appropriate advanced intervention to salvage ischemic tissue beyond standard rewarming?

options.A: Emergency surgical debridement and skin grafting within 24 hours
options.B: Intra-arterial or IV tPA (thrombolytic therapy) within 24 hours of rewarming
options.C: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for 90-minute sessions for 5 days
options.D: Immediate amputation of digits with absent perfusion on scan

questions.explanation: Severe frostbite (Grade 3-4) with absent perfusion on technetium bone scan or angiography indicates vascular thrombosis. The key principle: 'Frostbite in January, amputate in July' — never amputate early as tissue viability cannot be determined until full demarcation occurs (weeks-months). Advanced intervention: Intra-arterial or IV tPA (tissue plasminogen activator) administered within 24 hours of rewarming can lyse microthrombi in digital vessels and significantly improve tissue salvage rates. Standard care: rapid rewarming in water at 37-40°C, ibuprofen (anti-PGE2), aloe vera on blisters, avoid refreezing. Iloprost (prostacyclin analogue) is an alternative vasodilator agent.
